disease_info: Bipolar I Disorder is characterized by at least one lifetime manic episode, often alternating with episodes of major depression, leading to marked impairment in social or occupational functioning or the need for hospitalization. Manic episodes involve a sustained period of abnormally elevated, expansive, or irritable mood with increased energy and activity, while depressive episodes feature low mood and reduced interest or pleasure, along with changes in sleep, appetite, energy, and cognition. The course is typically recurrent and episodic, with symptom-free intervals of varying length, and onset commonly occurs in late adolescence or early adulthood but can present or re-emerge later in life. It is distinguished from Bipolar II Disorder by the presence of full mania (rather than hypomania) and from unipolar depression by a history of manic symptoms, and it often has significant consequences for relationships, work, and physical health if not adequately treated.

narrative.personality: Laura is a meticulous, imaginative, and somewhat anxious planner who takes pride in careful preparation and nurturing others through structured creative activities.
narrative.stressor: In the past year, Laura underwent a series of medical evaluations after a minor fall and some ambiguous test results suggested possible cardiac issues, which sharply intensified her longstanding worries about health and aging. Around the same time, several close colleagues from her teaching days experienced serious illnesses, forcing her to confront her own vulnerability and fueling a sense that she had to "make the most" of whatever time remained. She gradually shifted from her previously balanced routines into increasingly ambitious mentoring projects and community art initiatives, piling on responsibilities and restructuring her days, until her usual careful organization gave way to erratic schedules and obvious strain on her marriage and physical stamina. When her husband and adult daughter noticed that her movements, pacing, and activity level had become markedly different from her baseline and that she seemed unable to slow down or rest despite becoming exhausted and disorganized, they persuaded her to see a psychiatrist.
narrative.chief_complaint: My husband says I’ve been moving and pacing non-stop and just can’t seem to slow my body down.

narrative.personality: Ida is a structured, tender‑hearted woman who finds comfort in routine, careful planning, and nurturing her community through organized, detail‑oriented projects.
narrative.stressor: About six months ago, Ida lost her older sister, who had been her closest confidante and partner in genealogy projects and church activities, after a brief and unexpected illness. The bereavement disrupted the predictable rhythms she relied on, leaving long stretches of unstructured time and a sense that her carefully curated family history work no longer had its anchor. Initially she tried to cope by throwing herself into organizing the historical society’s archives and church events, but over several weeks this overextension gave way to a gradual retreat from her garden, quilting circle, and library volunteering as these activities began to feel burdensome and hollow. When her husband and fellow church choir members noticed that she had stopped showing up for rehearsals, left her canning supplies untouched, and no longer seemed interested in the projects that once animated her days, they encouraged her to seek professional help.
narrative.chief_complaint: I just don’t care about my garden, my quilting, or any of the things I used to love doing anymore.

narrative.personality: Kendall is an energetic, creatively restless person who thrives on spontaneity and new ideas but struggles with structure, deadlines, and follow‑through.
narrative.stressor: Kendall’s difficulties began after a series of overlapping project commitments and failed grant applications for her arts administration work left her feeling both pressured to prove herself and frustrated with traditional career paths. In response, she impulsively took on multiple pop‑up exhibition concepts at once, convinced she could parlay them into a breakout opportunity, and began staying up later and later planning events, networking, and sketching ideas without any real rest or schedule. Over several months, the initial rush of creative momentum devolved into chaotic days, mounting conflicts with collaborators over missed deadlines, and a growing inability to sustain her usual social and volunteer activities, leaving her feeling worn down in a way that even unstructured weekends and cutting back on obligations did not relieve. When her spouse noticed that she was constantly exhausted, dragging through basic tasks, and no longer able to muster the energy for even casual outings despite being out of the workforce, they urged her to see a psychiatrist.
narrative.chief_complaint: I feel completely drained all the time, like no amount of sleep or rest ever gives me my energy back.
